KEY MESSAGE 1: Below normal temperatures this week as high 
pressure prevails and a powerful nor'easter meanders off the 
Mid- Atlantic coast.

Through Tonight: The synoptic pattern has changed little in the
past 24 hours characterized by a slowly deepening nor'easter 
centered about 300 miles southeast of Cape Hatteras and
expansive high pressure building south over the entire 
Southeast U.S. and Deep South. The surface cyclone will 
gradually become more vertically stacked with its upper-level 
counterpart over the next 12-24 hours and gradually occlude 
based on the evolution of the 1000-500 hPa thickness ridging 
pattern and related gradients.

The nor'easter is forecast to gradually meander offshore of the
North Carolina Outer Banks through tonight. Locally, high 
pressure will prevail keeping the dry, fall weather in place 
across the Lowcountry and Southeast Georgia. Some low-level 
cloudiness spreading in from off the Atlantic this morning will 
bring some cloud cover for areas south of I-16 and possibly
along parts of the lower South Carolina coast, but as the main 
steering flow gradually backs with time, these clouds should mix
out as even drier air to the north advects into the region.
Sunny to mostly sunny skies are expected with highs warming 
into the 67-72 degree range (values right at the Third Quartile 
of the 19/01z NBM interquartile range/IQR), warmest along/south 
of the I-16 corridor and nudging up into the US-17 corridor into
parts of the Charleston Metro Area. Gusty north winds that have
plagued the region for the past few days will gradually wane
this afternoon as the surface high builds even farther to the 
south and the tightest pressure gradient between it and the 
nor'easter shifts farther offshore. Much lighter winds are
expected overnight and the boundary layer may even fully 
decouple in some locations resulting in light/variable to calm 
winds. This opens up the possibility for some modest radiational
cooling to occur given the dry airmass in place and ongoing 
clear skies. Lows were adjusted down a bit off the 19/01z NBM as
a result, ranging from the lower 40s well inland and up into 
the Francis Marion National Forest to the mid-upper 40s along 
the coastal corridor with lower-mid 50s at the beaches and 
Downtown Charleston.

Tuesday through Sunday: A nor'easter will be located well off 
the coast of NC Tuesday morning. Meanwhile, strong High pressure
will be located north of the Great Lakes region, with it's 
periphery stretching well down into the Southeast U.S. The 
nor'easter will very slowly shift away from our region through 
Thursday, then accelerate away Friday into the weekend. Though, 
the periphery of the distant High will persist across the 
Southeast U.S. This will bring our area dry conditions with 
sunny skies. MOS, 850 mb temperatures, and low-level thickness 
values, support high temperatures in the middle to maybe upper 
70s Tuesday and Wednesday, and the lower to middle 70s Thursday 
into the weekend. However, the dry conditions, clear skies, and 
light to calm winds at night will cause decent radiational 
cooling. This will lead to low temperatures that are several 
degrees below normal this week.


KEY MESSAGE 2: Risk for high surf will end this morning along 
much of the Georgia coast. High risk for rip currents for all 
beaches through this evening. 

High Surf: The risk for 5+ ft breakers will linger along the 
middle and upper Georgia coast through early afternoon. After 
that, the risk for high surf wane a bit as seas offshore 
gradually diminish. A High Surf Advisory is in effect for the 
beaches along the middle and upper Georgia coast through 2 PM.

The last several NWPS runs have shown larger breaking wave 
heights (4-7 ft) occurring along the Charleston County beaches 
later this afternoon into tonight with the arrival of a more 
powerful, higher period (~12 sec) back-swell. This is even as 
seas offshore slowly subside. Surf shop reports out of Folly 
Beach Sunday reported messy breakers of 3-4 ft, so it would not 
take much of an increase in swell period and/or swell power to 
breach the 5 ft High Surf Advisory criteria. If these model
trends persist, a High Surf Advisory may need to be issued for 
the Charleston County beaches to cover the mid afternoon into 
the Tuesday morning time period. Guidance does show breakers 
closer to 4-5 ft occurring farther down along the remainder of
the lower South Carolina and Georgia coasts as the long period 
swell train works to the southwest, so the need for an advisory 
there looks a bit more marginal.

Rip Currents: 
Today: The combination of gusty winds and elevated, lingering 
back- swell will support a high risk for rip currents at all 
beaches through this evening.

Tuesday: Strong and gusty N winds at daybreak will ease during
